summary: Documents a Cisco-developed, widely deployed measurement protocol for network performance, including latency, delay variation, and packet loss, using UDP probes. It was published so other vendors could interoperate. It is informational, not an Internet standard.

plainLanguage.summary: To measure how healthy a network is, an operator sends synthetic probes and times the replies. This RFC describes the probe protocol Cisco built and deployed widely, so that other vendors can interoperate with it. It covers the setup handshake, the format of each probe and reply, and the registries that make the protocol extensible.

subtitle: A vendor protocol for measuring latency, delay variation and packet loss with synthetic UDP probes, published so others can interoperate.

tldr.problem: Operators need to measure latency, delay variation and packet loss in a live network, and they need the measurements to be comparable between equipment from different vendors.
tldr.mechanism: The protocol has two phases: a control phase where the Sender asks the Responder to open a UDP port and authenticates itself, and a measurement phase of repeated request and response pairs whose timestamps and clock offsets produce the statistics.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational document describing a vendor protocol that has been widely deployed, published so that other implementations can interoperate rather than because the IETF standardised it.

facts.label: CSLD sections in a Control-Request
facts.value: At least 2: the Authentication CSLD and a Measurement-Type CSLD

today: RFC 6812 is an Informational document, and the metadata shows no obsoleting and no updating RFC. It is published as a contribution to the RFC Series, independently of any RFC stream, and describes a vendor protocol so that other implementations can interoperate with it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Active network performance measurements are becoming critical data points for administrators monitoring the health of the network. As service providers look to differentiate their offerings, performance measurement is increasingly becoming an important tool to monitor service-level guarantees and, in general, to monitor the health of a network.

Performance metrics, both one-way and two-way, can be used for pre-deployment validation as well as for measuring in-band live network-performance characteristics, and can measure service levels in L2 and L3 networks as well as for applications running on top of L3. Active performance measurements are gathered by analyzing synthetically generated request and response packets or frames. This is in contrast to passive measurements that analyze live traffic flowing through a particular network element.

There is a growing body of work on Performance Measurement standards that enable interoperability between different vendors' network elements by describing common measurement protocols as well as metrics, and the IETF has actively developed Standards Track documents on the subject, such as A One-way Active Measurement Protocol and the Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol.

Cisco's SLA Protocol is another example of a Performance Measurement protocol that offers a rich set of measurement message types. The measurement types can be classified as those that test connectivity, in a ping-like way, by providing round-trip or one-way latency measures, and those that provide a richer set of statistics including network jitter and packet or frame loss. Each type of active measurement exchange mimics an actual protocol exchange. The UDP-Measurement message exchanges simulate a UDP application and can be used to simulate either Voice or Video traffic encoded in RTP frames within UDP envelopes, and they carry information that provides the ability to derive a robust set of statistics.
sections.plainLanguage: To measure how healthy a network is, an operator sends synthetic probes and times the replies. This RFC describes the probe protocol Cisco built and deployed widely, so that other vendors can interoperate with it. It covers the setup handshake, the format of each probe and reply, and the registries that make the protocol extensible.

sections.title: The Two Phases of the Protocol
sections.content:
The protocol consists of two distinct phases, the Control Phase and the Measurement Phase. Each phase is comprised of information exchanged between a network element acting as the Sender and an element designated as the Responder.

The Control Phase is the first phase of message exchanges and forms the base protocol. It establishes the identity of the Sender and provides information for the Measurement Phase, and a single message pair of Control-Request and Control-Response marks this phase. The Sender initiates a Control-Request, which is acknowledged by the Responder with a Control-Response. The Control-Request may be sent multiple times if a Control-Response has not been received, and the number of times the message is retried is configurable on the Sender element.

The Control-Request message is sent to UDP port 1167 on the Responder, requesting that a Measurement Phase UDP port be opened, and it indicates the duration for which that port needs to remain open. The Responder replies by sending a Control-Response with an appropriate Status indicating Success when the Sender identity is verified and the requested UDP port was successfully opened. In all other cases, a non-zero Status is returned in the Command-Header Status field.

The Measurement Phase forms the second phase and is comprised of a sequence of Measurement-Request and Measurement-Response messages, which may be exchanged as often as required. Each Measurement-Request message is acknowledged by the Responder with a Measurement-Response message. The number and frequency with which messages are sent should be controlled by configuration on the Sender element, along with the waiting time for a Control-Response.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two rounds. First a handshake: the sender asks the responder to open a UDP port and proves who it is. Then the measuring starts, with a request and a response repeated as often as configured.

sections.title: The Control-Request Message
sections.content:
The Control-Request message consists of a Command-Header followed by one or more Command, Status, Length and Data sections, henceforth known as CSLD. At a minimum there should be two CSLD sections, one of which is the authentication CSLD section and the other carries information for the Measurement Phase simulation type.

The Command-Header is the first section of the message. It carries a Version field of 8 bits, set to 2; a Reserved field of 8 bits, which must be set to 0; a Status field of 16 bits, which indicates success or failure for the entire message and, in a Control-Request, is ignored by the receiver and should be set to 0; a Sequence Number of 32 bits, used to map requests to responses, which is monotonically increasing and must remain unchanged when a Control-Request is retried; a Total Length field of 32 bits, carrying the total length of the Control message in octets; and a Send Timestamp of 64 bits, set to the time the command was submitted for transmission and updated for a response. The timestamp may be used when security is of concern in order to prevent replay attacks, and when not being used it must be set to all zeros. The format is as given in RFC 5905.

The ordered list of the two CSLDs to be included along with the Command-Header are the Authentication CSLD and a Measurement-Type CSLD. In this revision of the protocol only a single Measurement-Type CSLD has been defined, the UDP-Measurement CSLD, though more may be added in future.

The Authentication CSLD provides message authentication and verifies that the requester knows the shared secret. It carries a Mode field, a Key Id, a Random Number and a Message Authentication Digest. The Random Number field is used to prevent dictionary attacks and is to be set to a random value in environments where security is a concern. An implementation must include the Random Number and Message Authentication fields when the mode is non-zero, and may include them when the mode is set to No Authentication, in which case they must be set to zero. For the SHA256 authenticator mode, the shared secret is prepended to the Control message and the authentication algorithm is run over the complete data including the shared secret. That mode is included for ease of implementation, and use of the HMAC variant is strongly recommended for stronger security.

The UDP-Measurement CSLD indicates the Measurement-Type to be used during the Measurement Phase and specifies the addresses and UDP port to be opened, as well as the duration that the port has to be kept open. It carries an Address Type, where 2 means IPv4 and 3 means IPv6; a Role, where 1 means Responder; a Session Identifier; the control source, control destination, measurement source and measurement destination addresses, each 128 bits with the remaining bits zeroed for IPv4; the control source port, the measurement source port and the measurement destination port; and a Duration in milliseconds, which is how long the port needs to be kept open for accepting Measurement Phase messages. Measurement messages received after the duration must be ignored. If the UDP port indicated in the UDP-Measurement CSLD is busy, the Responder may suggest an alternative port, in which case the Status of the UDP-Measurement CSLD must be set to Success.
sections.plainLanguage: Every control message starts with a fixed header and then a list of sections, each with a command code, a status, a length and some data. Two are required: one proving the sender's identity with a shared secret, and one describing the measurement to come and the UDP port it should use.

sections.title: The Measurement Phase
sections.content:
Each Measurement-Request carries the type of measurement being performed, where 1 and 2 are Reserved and 3 is UDP-Measurement; a Reserved field that must be set to 0; a Sender Send Time of 64 bits, the timestamp when the measurement message was submitted for transmission by the Sender; a Responder Receive Time of 64 bits, the timestamp when the measurement message was received by the Responder; a Responder Send Time of 64 bits, which must be 0 in the Sender-to-Responder direction; a Sender Receive Time of 64 bits, which must be 0 in both directions on the wire and is filled on the Sender side as soon as the measurement message is received; a Sender Clock Offset and a Responder Clock Offset, each 64 bits giving an estimate of the clock skew measured in seconds and fractional seconds; a Sender Sequence Number and a Responder Sequence Number, each 32 bits, monotonically increasing and allowed to wrap around; and a Data field used to pad up to the configured request data size, whose minimum size should be 64 octets.

All timestamps have the default format described in RFC 5905: the first 32 bits are the unsigned integer number of seconds elapsed since 0 h on 1 January 1900, and the next 32 bits are the fractional part of a second. An alternative format is also permitted, the truncated 64-bit form of the IEEE 1588-2008 Precision Time Protocol timestamp, which consists of a 32-bit seconds field followed by a 32-bit nanoseconds field. Implementations must use only one of the two formats, and the chosen format is negotiated out of band between the endpoints or defaults to the RFC 5905 format.

Several implementation notes apply. Responder implementations should support simultaneous measurements destined to a single port, either from the same or a different Sender, and for different measurement instances that originate from the same Sender there must be a clear method for the Responder to distinguish the traffic, for example per a unique 5-tuple of protocol, source address, source port, destination address and destination port. A Control-Request received for the same Measurement-Type request, as identified by the 5-tuples, should result in the resetting of the duration timer and the Responder sequence number. A Control Phase followed by the Measurement Phase can be repeated in order to have a continuous measurement over the entire lifetime of a device.

The measurement stream typically consists of packets or frames with a periodic inter-packet distribution. The Sender need not wait for a Measurement-Response packet to arrive before sending another Measurement-Request packet, and in many cases it will not be possible to wait in order to maintain the desired inter-packet distribution. All messages and fields within a message are assumed to be in network order, and all data fields are unsigned unless mentioned otherwise.
sections.plainLanguage: Each probe carries the times it was sent and received, plus an estimate of how far the two clocks are apart. That is what turns the probes into latency, jitter and loss figures. The sender keeps sending probes on a schedule without waiting for each reply.

sections.title: Registries for Extensibility
sections.content:
The RFC defines a set of registries that the protocol needs to be extensible, and in them the terms Private Use and Experimental Use have the same meaning as described in RFC 5226. For the version, CSLD command, authenticator mode, role and measurement type registries, the ranges designated Unassigned are governed by the policy RFC Required.

The Version Number registry reserves 0 and 1, assigns 2 to Version 2, leaves 3 to 200 Unassigned, and sets aside 201 to 225 for Private Use and 226 to 255 for Experimental Use. The version number should be changed only when the structure of the Command messages differs from the basic Command-Header and CSLD structure described in the document.

The CSLD Command registry reserves 0, assigns 1 to the Authentication CSLD and 2 to UDP-Measurement, reserves 3 to 52, leaves 53 to 10239 Unassigned, and sets aside 10240 to 20479 for Private Use and 20480 to 65535 for Experimental Use. It is envisioned that future documents will provide their own Measurement-Type number and format of the Data portion.

The Authenticator Modes registry sets 0 to No Authentication, 1 to SHA256 and 2 to HMAC-SHA-256. The Roles registry sets 1 to Sender and 2 to Responder. The Measurement Type registry reserves 0, 1 and 2 and assigns 3 to UDP.

Two further registries use different policies. The Status Types registry, governed by First Come First Served, sets 0 to Success, 1 to Fail as a catch-all, 2 to Authentication failure, 3 to Format error, sent when any CSLD type is not recognized or any part of a CSLD has an unrecognized value, and 4 to Port in use, meaning the UDP or TCP port is already being used by some other application and cannot be reserved. The Address Family registry, governed by Specification Required, sets 2 to IPv4 and 3 to IPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: Every number the protocol carries is drawn from a published list, so that a new measurement type or a new status code can be added later without breaking anything that already exists.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
When the mode for the Authentication CSLD is set to 1, the Message Authentication Digest is generated using the SHA256 algorithm and is calculated over the entire packet including the Message Authentication Digest field, which must be set to all zeros. When the mode is set to 2, the digest is generated using the HMAC-SHA-256 algorithm as described in RFC 4868, again over the entire packet including the digest field, which must be set to all zeros. When the mode field is set to 0, the Random Number and the Message Authentication Digest fields may be included, and when present they must be set to all zeros.

It is recommended that IPsec be employed to afford better security. IPsec provides enhanced privacy as well as an automated key-distribution mechanism. For Senders, the IPsec policy would be to initiate IPsec from the Sender to any Responder, destination port UDP 1167, which causes the Sender to initiate IPsec when sending control traffic to any Responder; if some Responders do not support IPsec, a more granular policy is required. For Responders, the policy would be to require IPsec from any to the Responder, destination port UDP 1167, and a more granular policy is again needed if some Sender does not support IPsec.

For measurement traffic, because the Control Phase occurs before the Measurement Phase, it should be possible to build an IPsec Security Association once a successful Control-Response is received. The Sender policy would then be to initiate IPsec from the Sender to the negotiated address, destination the negotiated port, and the Responder policy to require IPsec from the negotiated address to the Responder, destination the negotiated port.

For replay protection, the originator of a Control message may choose to include a current value in the Send Timestamp field indicating the time the message was submitted for transmission; otherwise it must be set to 0. The receiver may choose to validate it if the timestamp is within an acceptable range. The measurement traffic described in the document contains a timestamp indicating the sent time, so no new field is required for it.
sections.plainLanguage: The shared secret can protect the setup messages, and IPsec is recommended to protect both the setup and the measurement traffic. The send timestamp is there so that an old message cannot be replayed later.

fields.desc: Maps requests to responses. Monotonically increasing, and unchanged when a request is retried.

fields.desc: Total length of the Control message in octets.

fields.desc: Time the command was submitted for transmission, in the RFC 5905 format. Set to all zeros when not used.
